attributes.source_locator: Sections 2.3, 3.2 and 4.3
attributes.value: Section 2.3: 'Additionally, EGF and Cetuximab were run as positive controls.' Section 3.2: 'Cetuximab was also used as a positive control in the competition (9.94 nM), allowing for the calculation that this represents an 8.2 x improvement.' Section 4.3: 'Two R2 binders have KD values on par or better than Cetuximab.' Cetuximab is an approved therapeutic antibody obtained by conventional antibody discovery, so its 9.94 nM in this assay is a reference point for what a conventional binder achieves on EGFR, measured on the same instrument as the designs. It is not evidence about the hit rate of conventional methods, because no library selection campaign was run and no candidate set was tested.

description: The Adaptyv assay ran EGF and cetuximab as positive controls, and cetuximab measured 9.94 nM. This is the only same-assay measurement of a conventionally obtained binder in any source this pass retrieved. It is a control for assay validity, not a design-method arm: there is no candidate set and no denominator behind it.
name: Cetuximab, obtained by conventional means, measured 9.94 nM in the same assay

attributes.source_locator: Section S4.1
attributes.value: Section S4.1, verbatim: 'Published experimental success rates of RFdiffusion were based on 96-well biolayer interferometry (BLI) measurements [S28], which are impractical for us to perform on our own designs. Therefore, to quantitatively compare success rates, we downloaded sequences of the published RFdiffusion designs and synthesized and tested them by yeast display (Section S1.2) alongside our own designs. Our results matched the published success rates for PD-L1 but were 2-fold lower for IL-7RA (16% versus 33%) and 0% for TrkA (versus 6%) (Table S2). This is potentially due to differences between the yeast surface environment versus purified proteins, as well as our use of 10- to 20-fold lower target concentrations (0.5-1 uM versus 10 uM in [S28]), which may exclude lower-affinity hits.' Section S4.1 therefore states a shared assay and does not state a shared selection funnel: the AlphaProteo candidates were chosen by the authors' own filter from a larger in silico set, while the RFdiffusion candidates are the 95 designs the RFdiffusion authors published.

description: The AlphaProteo authors did not run RFdiffusion. Section S4.1 states that they downloaded the published RFdiffusion design sequences and synthesised and tested those by yeast display alongside their own designs, because the published RFdiffusion rates rest on 96-well BLI measurements that were impractical for them to perform.
name: Section S4.1 states that the RFdiffusion arm is the published designs re-tested, not a rerun

attributes.value: Results 'Improved oracles increase success rate', verbatim: 'We found that the AlphaFold3 interface predicted template modelling (ipTM) score, a measure of model confidence over the interface, is predictive of binding success (area under the curve = 0.86; Extended Data Fig. 10a,b). Overall, only 9% of our ordered VHH designs have an ipTM > 0.6, suggesting that success rate will be improved by incorporation of an ipTM filter.' And for the scFv libraries: 'Only 4% of the initial design library has ipTM > 0.85, whereas 5 out of the 6 experimentally confirmed designs pass this threshold.' The paper also states that the fine-tuned RoseTTAFold2 filter's 'filtering power ... is limited (at least with the settings used; providing 100% of interface hotspots)' and that this 'probably accounts for the low experimental success rates'.

description: The paper's retrospective analysis finds that AlphaFold3 interface pTM separates binders from non-binders with an area under the curve of 0.86, and that only 9% of the ordered VHH designs have ipTM above 0.6, so the tested set was chosen by a filter the authors now consider weak.
name: Only 9% of the ordered Bennett VHH designs have AlphaFold3 ipTM above 0.6

The tested set is not a sample of any method's output: half the round-1 and three quarters of the round-2 tested designs were hand-picked by the organisers for diversity, and entrants chose how many designs to submit and how much effort to spend.
Design methods are the entrants' own declarations, curated by the organisers into five categories.

Sequences yielding under 0.02 micrograms per millilitre of protein were excluded before characterisation, so the binding denominator is the expressed set for some statements and the selected set for others.

attributes.protocol: Submitted sequences are reverse-translated and codon-optimised, expressed in a cell-free system in at least two batches, and quantified by a label-free assay. Sequences yielding less than 0.02 micrograms per millilitre are excluded. Expressed ligands are immobilised by tag-specific chemistry and EGFR is flowed over the probe at 1000 nM to 10 nM in a multi-cycle kinetic assay, in duplicate, in HBS-T with 0.5% BSA at 25 degrees Celsius. Signals are baseline-corrected and fitted with a 1:1 binding model; where the maximum signal is below the quantifiable threshold or the kinetics are too fast, equilibrium analysis is used instead. A minimum of two replicates was run for each design, and EGF and cetuximab were run as positive controls.

limitations: Third-party assay: Adaptyv expressed and measured the designs, so the measurement is independent of the design methods. The organisers wrote the paper.
No hit definition is printed. Section 4.1 refers to 'the 3 binding thresholds' in Figure 8 and no section of the paper defines them.

The tested set is not a sample of any method's output: half the round-1 and three quarters of the round-2 tested designs were hand-picked by the organisers for diversity, and entrants chose how many designs to submit and how much effort to spend.
Design methods are the entrants' own declarations, curated by the organisers into five categories.

Sequences yielding under 0.02 micrograms per millilitre of protein were excluded before characterisation, so the binding denominator is the expressed set for some statements and the selected set for others.
No conventional comparator arm. EGF and cetuximab were positive controls.
No uncertainty is printed for any rate.
Section 2.4 gives the round 2 expression rate as 95% (378 of 400) and Section 4.1 gives it as 94%.
attributes.metric_qualifier: designs that expressed above the 0.02 microgram per millilitre threshold, out of designs selected for testing
attributes.protocol: Submitted sequences are reverse-translated, codon-optimised and expressed in a cell-free system over at least two batches, with some sequences tested up to four times. Expression success is assessed by a label-free quantification assay; sequences yielding less than 0.02 micrograms per millilitre are excluded from further characterisation.
attributes.source_locator: Sections 2.4 and 4.1; round 2 repository README, 'Protein Synthesis'

limitations: Developer-reported: the authors built AlphaProteo, chose the targets, ran the assay and chose which designs to test.

A hit is a flow-cytometry binding signal above a manually calibrated threshold, not an affinity. The thresholds 'were calibrated manually by visually inspecting scatterplots of the raw yeast data' (Section S1.2.1).
The designs tested were chosen by the authors' own automated filter from a larger in silico set, so the design step and the selection step are coupled.
Denominators are small (30 to 172 designs per target) and no uncertainty is printed.
No conventional comparator (directed evolution, display selection or grafting) was run on these targets.
Target concentrations were 0.5 to 1 micromolar, 10- to 20-fold lower than in the RFdiffusion publication, 'which may exclude lower-affinity hits' (Section S4.1).

attributes.protocol: Designs are codon-optimised, synthesised and transformed into S. cerevisiae EBY100, displayed on the surface, incubated with biotinylated target protein, and read by flow cytometry. The binding signal is (log10 PE[FITC+,+target] - log10 PE[FITC-,+target]) - (log10 PE[FITC+,-target] - log10 PE[FITC-,-target]). Designs with a binding signal above 0.2 were considered successful binders.
attributes.selection: Between 47 and 172 candidates per target chosen by the authors' automated filtering procedure from a larger in silico set.
attributes.selection_bias: The filter that chose the tested designs is the authors' own, so design and selection are not independent.

limitations: Developer-reported: the BindCraft authors built the pipeline, chose the targets and chose which designs to test.

The assay is not uniform across targets. Fig. 1b's caption says binding was observed on SPR, but PD-1 was screened by BLI in a bivalent Fc-fusion format and the claudin binders were prescreened against soluble analogues of the target rather than the wild-type protein.
No numeric binding threshold is stated. A successful design is one where a binding signal was observed.

evidence_concerns.message: The paper prints three different round-1 binder rates and two round-2 expression rates. Section 2.4 gives round 1 as '2.5% (5/201)' and round 2 as 'a 95% expression rate (378 of 400 tested)'; Section 4.1 gives expression as improving 'from 73% to 94%'; Section 4.2 gives the binder percentage as rising 'from 3% in the first round to 13%'. All the printed values are recorded with their locators and none is reconciled here.

Section 4.1 says Figure 8 shows 'the total number of validated binders across the 3 binding thresholds' but no section of the paper defines those three thresholds. No hit definition is therefore recorded for the Figure 8 counts, and the binding protocol's success threshold is left unstated with a reason rather than guessed.

attributes.rationale: Before machine-learning design, a new binder to a chosen target came from iterated selection: directed evolution, phage or yeast display from a naive or immunised library, or grafting a known binding motif from a solved complex. Those are what a design workflow replaces, so they are the reference. The evidence this pass retrieved contains no such arm on any target a design method was also run on. Its only same-assay trace is cetuximab, an approved antibody obtained by conventional discovery, measured at 9.94 nM as a positive control in the Adaptyv EGFR assay, and AlphaProteo's Table 1 caption states that 'binders derived from selection-based methods, such as antibodies and nanobodies, are not considered here'. The baseline is therefore recorded as named but unmeasured, and the absence of a comparator is the use case's primary evidence gap.

attributes.clinical_scope: Research only. A measured binding outcome does not establish efficacy, developability, immunogenicity or clinical suitability, and nothing here supports any therapeutic use of a designed binder.

baselines: Directed evolution or library display selection from a naive library on the same target
Grafting from a solved complex with a known binder, where one exists
collection_plan.comparison_question: On the same targets, with one expression and assay pipeline and one hit definition, how does the share of designs that bind differ between two design workflows and a conventional comparator at the same testing budget?
collection_plan.next_step: Retrieve BenchBB and ProtDBench to establish whether a standing binder design benchmark with a fixed hit definition exists, and run a separate literature pass for conventional display and directed-evolution arms on any target that a design paper also reports.
outcomes: Share of designs that bind at a single stated threshold on one assay, with the denominator
Affinity distribution of the binders found, not only the best one
The full funnel: designs generated, ordered, expressed, assayed and confirmed
Designs that had to be made per binder obtained, at a fixed budget
validation_requirements: Fix the hit definition before the comparison and apply it to every arm.
Separate the design step from the selection step: report the rate over a random sample of generated designs as well as over the filter's top picks.
Match the targets across arms and state for each whether it has a known binder or a solved complex.
Report the denominator and an interval for every rate.
Keep modalities apart: miniprotein, antibody variable domain and peptide results are not interchangeable.

attributes.decision: Choose a computational design workflow for a new target, and decide how many designs to synthesise and assay.
evidence_gaps: No conventional comparator exists in the retrieved evidence. Not one of the sources runs directed evolution, library display selection or grafting from a known complex on the same targets as a design method, with the same expression and assay pipeline and the same hit definition. This is the primary gap and it cannot be closed by extracting more of these papers; it needs a pass over the display and directed-evolution literature, or a measurement.
No source anywhere runs two design methods and a conventional comparator on the same targets with one assay and one hit definition, so the use case's own question cannot currently be answered.
BenchBB (benchbb.bio) was not retrieved. Its seven-target list, protocol, assay and whether any method has been run on it are unknown, and no results on BenchBB were found for any method.

ProtDBench (arXiv:2605.04118 v2) was not retrieved; only its abstract was read in the search pass. It is the only candidate standing benchmark for binder design found, and nothing is claimed about it here.

The single-target binder design literature was not retrieved. The search pass surfaced a large population of one-off papers, each reporting a hit rate for one target with its own assay (Francisella virulence factor, deltacoronavirus, Nipah, Langya and measles receptor-binding domains, GDF15-GFRAL, RH5, canine and human TNF-alpha, HSP90, CCL25, BRD3). Taken together they are the largest untapped pool of measured outcomes and the place where publication bias will be worst.

Adaptyv per-method and per-category hit rates were not extracted. The round 2 repository publishes one row per design with a binding flag and an affinity, but neither the repository nor the paper states an aggregation over those rows, the method labels are entrants' free text, and the three binding thresholds behind the Figure 8 counts are never defined.
The Adaptyv round 1 repository, raw kinetic curve package, neutralisation package and structure predictions were not retrieved, and the 60 measured affinities in Figure 10 were not read.

BindCraft's per-target numerators for CrSAS-6 and CbAgo were not obtained. They are printed only inside the Figure 1b graphic, which was not read, and Supplementary Data 1 does not let them be recomputed: the row filter that reconciles with the prose for nine targets fails for PD-L1, CrSAS-6 and CbAgo.

BoltzGen (bioRxiv 10.1101/2025.11.20.689494) Tables 2 and 3 were not extracted. It reports a cold-start against warm-start split (6 of 9 novel targets against 4 of 5 benchmark targets with known binders) that is exactly the protocol limit the use case needs, and some of its data are stated to be temporarily confidential.

Filius et al. 2025 (ACS Chem Biol 10.1021/acschembio.5c00774) Supporting Information Table S3 was not extracted. It is a third-party wet-lab test of BindCraft on four targets that reports the two targets which failed outright, which is the kind of independent evidence this use case is shortest of.

The Nature Communications minibinder paper (doi 10.1038/s41467-026-76760-5) was not extracted. It is the closest thing found to an independent replication: one group, one assay, three targets of differing difficulty with the same method.

PXDesign's own measured values (bioRxiv 10.1101/2025.08.15.670450, Tables 1 and 2) were not extracted. Its baseline column is deliberately excluded: those numbers are copied from publications and partly adjusted by the PXDesign authors using their own HTRF data, which is a third party's reanalysis.

The values in AlphaProteo's 'Other design methods' rows and its 'RFdiffusion (published)' row are recorded only as a transcription claim, not as results, for the same reason: they are copied from publications this pass did not retrieve, and Section S4.2 states that the asterisked values were re-measured by the AlphaProteo authors and that for PD-L1 they substituted a different design for the published best one. The primary sources behind those cells (Procko et al., Gainza et al., Cao et al., Berger et al., Yang et al., Watson et al.) were not retrieved.

Junker and Schoeder 2026 (PLOS ONE 10.1371/journal.pone.0355549) is the most careful cross-method comparison found and has no wet-lab arm, so it supplies no outcome. Nanda 2026 (doi 10.21203/rs.3.rs-11106209/v1) on amyloid fibrils is likewise in silico only. Amyloid fibrils and GPCR peptide targets are target classes for which no measured binder design outcome was found at all.
No source reports uncertainty for any hit rate or affinity. Every rate in this use case is a point value over a denominator between 6 and 9,000, with no interval.
No source connects a designed binder to a downstream outcome such as efficacy, developability or manufacturability.
Automated source review only. Independent human scientific review remains outstanding, and nothing here has been experimentally replicated.
exclusions: Hit definitions are not commensurable across these sources. A yeast-display flow-cytometry signal above 0.2, a BLI KD below 1000 nM, an SPR response at half the positive control, and 'nanomolar with a human serum albumin counter-screen' are four different endpoints, and the hit rate moves by tens of percentage points depending on which is used.

Denominators are small and author-selected, and the designs tested are the top-ranked ones by each method's own filter, so the design step and the selection step are coupled. Changing only the filter moved AlphaProteo's PD-L1 rate from 9.6% over 94 designs to 16.1% over 31.

The spread within a single method across targets is wider than any plausible difference between methods: AlphaProteo 0% to 88%, BindCraft 10% to 100%, Bennett 0% to 2% for antibodies. A method ranking built from these numbers would mostly be measuring which targets each group chose.

No source includes a conventional comparator (directed evolution, library display selection or grafting from a known complex) on the same targets as a design method. Cetuximab's 9.94 nM in the Adaptyv assay is a positive control for assay validity, not a comparator arm: no candidate set was tested and there is no denominator behind it.
The evidence here does not support a workflow recommendation. It supports per-method, per-target statements about what happened when designs were made and tested.

An in silico score (interface predicted aligned error, ipTM, predicted local distance difference test, self-consistency RMSD) is a filter inside the pipeline, not an outcome. Filter pass rates are recorded as outside the use case's endpoint.

Almost all of the measured evidence is author-reported by the group that built the method. Only the Adaptyv competition measurements are independent of the design methods, and they are on one target with no hit definition printed.
Research only. None of this evidence establishes therapeutic efficacy, developability or clinical suitability for any designed binder.

Whether the target has a known binder or a solved complex, which decides whether this is a cold start
The binder modality required: miniprotein, antibody variable domain, nanobody or peptide

Expression, solubility and format constraints on the designs that can be tested

attributes.source_locator: AlphaProteo Table 1, Table S2 and Sections S1.2.1, S2 and S4.1; BindCraft Introduction and Results prose; Bennett Supplementary Methods Table 6; Adaptyv Sections 2.3, 2.4, 3.1, 3.2, 4.1, 4.2 and 4.3
attributes.value:
Nine sources carry measured outcomes for de novo binder design and none of them answers which workflow to use, because no paper runs two design methods and a conventional comparator on the same targets with one assay and one hit definition.

What the measured evidence shows is that the target matters more than the method. AlphaProteo's yeast-display success rate across eight targets runs from 0% over 54 designs on TNF-alpha to 88% over 94 designs on BHRF1, at a binding-signal threshold of 0.2 (1.3 on IL-17A). BindCraft reports an average experimental success rate of 46.3% over twelve targets with a range of 10% to 100%, built from per-target counts as small as 2 binders from 7 designs on Bet v1 and as large as 6 from 6 on the SpCas9 REC1 domain. The same family of methods applied to antibody variable domains is two orders of magnitude worse: fine-tuned RFdiffusion gives 2% over 96 designs on TcdB, 0% over 96 on IL-7 receptor alpha, and 0.01% to 0.2% over 9,000 designs per target by yeast display. On influenza H1 stem the same design campaign gives 1% over 96 designs by SPR and 0.2% over 9,000 by display, so the screening method moves the rate as much as the target does.

Nearly all of this is author-reported by the group that built the method, which also chose the targets, ran the assay and chose which designs to test. The exception is the Adaptyv EGFR competition, where a third-party laboratory expressed and measured designs from many entrants on one target and one assay: 2.5% of 201 round-1 designs bound (printed elsewhere in the same paper as 3%), and 53 of 400 round-2 designs bound, printed as 13%. That source cannot be turned into a per-method rate: design methods are the entrants' own declarations, the organisers hand-picked 101 of 201 round-1 and 300 of 400 round-2 designs for diversity, and the three binding thresholds behind the figure counts are never defined.

Affinities reached are better than the hit rates suggest. AlphaProteo's best measured binder was 0.082 nM on IL-7 receptor alpha by HTRF; BindCraft's best ranged from 5 nM on CbAgo to 5.7 micromolar on CrSAS-6; the best de novo design in the Adaptyv competition reached 82 nM and the winning optimised cetuximab fragment 1.21 nM, against 9.94 nM for the cetuximab positive control measured on the same instrument.

Three things stop these numbers from ranking methods. The hit definitions are different endpoints, not different thresholds on one endpoint. The denominators are small and chosen, and the designs tested are the top picks of each method's own filter, so design and selection are coupled: changing only AlphaProteo's filter moved its PD-L1 rate from 9.6% over 94 designs to 16.1% over 31, and the Bennett authors attribute their low antibody rates partly to a filter they describe as weak. And the spread within one method across targets is wider than any plausible difference between methods. No conventional comparator is run anywhere in this evidence, so there is no measurement of what a designed binder is being compared against.

description: A descriptive account of what the reviewed evidence shows about de novo binder design: the per-target spread, the antibody-versus-miniprotein gap, the author-reported nature of nearly all of it, and the absence of any controlled cross-method comparison. It makes no recommendation.
name: Summary of the de novo binder design evidence
